modules.title: ECOWAS
modules.html:
1. Formation

The Economic Community of West African States was established by the Treaty of Lagos on 28 May 1975, largely through the initiative of General Yakubu Gowon of Nigeria and President Gnassingbe Eyadema of Togo. It has fifteen member states with headquarters in Abuja; the revised treaty of 1993 broadened its mandate to political cooperation and security.

2. Aims and Objectives

  1. Promote cooperation and integration leading to an economic union in West Africa.
  2. Abolish customs duties and other trade barriers among members.
  3. Establish a common external tariff and commercial policy.
  4. Ensure free movement of persons, goods, services and capital, and the right of residence and establishment.
  5. Harmonise agricultural, industrial, transport, energy and monetary policies.
  6. Raise living standards and maintain economic stability.
  7. Maintain peace, security and democratic governance in the sub-region.

3. Organs

OrganFunction
Authority of Heads of State and GovernmentSupreme organ; sets policy, meets annually
Council of MinistersRecommends policy, supervises the Commission
ECOWAS Commission (formerly Executive Secretariat)Day-to-day administration, headed by a President of the Commission
Community ParliamentAdvisory representative assembly in Abuja
Community Court of JusticeInterprets the treaty; hears human-rights cases from citizens
EBID (ECOWAS Bank for Investment and Development)Finances projects and compensates members for losses from integration
Specialised commissionsTrade, industry, transport, social and cultural affairs, defence

4. Achievements

  • Free movement of persons within the sub-region, and the ECOWAS passport and travel certificate.
  • Removal of visa requirements for 90-day stays among members.
  • ECOMOG peacekeeping in Liberia (1990), Sierra Leone (1997), Guinea-Bissau, Cote d'Ivoire, Mali and the Gambia (2017, ECOMIG restoring the elected President Barrow).
  • Protocol on Democracy and Good Governance (2001) and automatic suspension of members after coups.
  • Trade Liberalisation Scheme; West African Power Pool and Gas Pipeline; ECOWAS Standby Force.
  • Regional collaboration on agriculture, health (Ebola and COVID-19 responses) and education.

5. Problems

  • Language and colonial-heritage divisions between anglophone, francophone and lusophone members, and francophone attachment to UEMOA and the CFA franc.
  • Political instability and repeated coups; the announced withdrawal of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger in 2024–2025 tested cohesion.
  • Non-implementation of protocols and persistent border harassment and checkpoints.
  • Similar, competing primary-product economies limiting intra-regional trade.
  • Poor transport and communication links; currency inconvertibility and the delayed single currency, the eco.
  • Financial arrears and dependence on Nigeria for funding.

examples.a: When Liberia's civil war spread in 1990, ECOWAS deployed ECOMOG, with Nigeria supplying the bulk of troops, commanders and finance. It stopped a massacre in Monrovia, created space for the Abuja peace accords and the 1997 elections, and pioneered African-led regional peace enforcement later copied by the AU. Criticisms: it lacked an explicit treaty mandate at the outset, francophone states questioned Nigerian dominance, ECOMOG troops were accused of profiteering, and the human and financial cost to Nigeria was enormous.

examples.q: Why has intra-ECOWAS trade remained low?
examples.a: Members produce similar primary commodities — cocoa, oil, groundnuts, timber — and therefore compete rather than complement each other; their trade is oriented towards former colonial powers. Add poor road and rail links, multiple currencies with limited convertibility, non-tariff barriers and checkpoints, smuggling, and slow implementation of the Trade Liberalisation Scheme, and formal intra-regional trade remains a small fraction of total trade.

modules.title: From the OAU to the African Union
modules.html:
1. The OAU, 1963–2002

Formed in Addis Ababa on 25 May 1963 by 32 states, compromising between the radical Casablanca group (Nkrumah's immediate political union) and the moderate Monrovia group (gradual functional cooperation, favoured by Nigeria).

Aims: promote unity and solidarity; coordinate cooperation for a better life; defend sovereignty and territorial integrity; eradicate colonialism; promote international cooperation under the UN Charter.

Achievements: decolonisation through the Liberation Committee, contribution to the end of apartheid, mediation in the Algeria–Morocco and Somalia–Ethiopia disputes, the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (1981), and a common African voice at the UN.

Weaknesses: strict non-interference allowed dictators to abuse citizens with impunity; no standing army; financial arrears; ideological and linguistic splits; the Western Sahara dispute; inability to prevent the Rwandan genocide.

2. The African Union, 2002

Proposed in the Sirte Declaration (1999), given legal form in the Constitutive Act (Lome, 2000) and launched at Durban in July 2002. Headquarters: Addis Ababa. Membership: 55 states.

3. Organs of the AU

OrganFunction
Assembly of Heads of State and GovernmentSupreme policy organ
Executive CouncilForeign ministers; prepares Assembly decisions
AU CommissionSecretariat headed by a Chairperson
Pan-African ParliamentRepresentative body sited in Midrand, South Africa
Peace and Security CouncilConflict prevention, management and resolution; authorises intervention
African Court on Human and Peoples' RightsAdjudicates human-rights cases
ECOSOCCAdvisory organ of civil society
Specialised agenciesAfrican Development Bank, NEPAD/AUDA, African Peer Review Mechanism

4. Key Differences from the OAU

  • The AU may intervene in a member state in grave circumstances — war crimes, genocide, crimes against humanity (Article 4(h)) — replacing absolute non-interference.
  • It suspends governments that come to power unconstitutionally.
  • It has stronger economic ambitions: AfCFTA (operational 2021), a projected monetary union and Agenda 2063.
  • It provides for a standby force and a Pan-African Parliament.

5. Problems

Funding arrears and dependence on external donors, weak enforcement of decisions, persistent coups and conflicts, poor intra-African trade infrastructure, and the gap between ambitious protocols and implementation.

examples.q: Explain the significance of Article 4(h) of the AU Constitutive Act.
examples.a: It gives the Union the right to intervene in a member state, pursuant to an Assembly decision, in respect of grave circumstances — war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity. This reverses the OAU's absolute doctrine of non-interference, which had left the Union powerless during the Rwandan genocide of 1994. It embodies the shift from 'non-interference' to 'non-indifference' and underpins AU peace-support deployments in Burundi, Darfur and Somalia.

examples.q: Contrast the Casablanca and Monrovia groups.
examples.a: The Casablanca group (Ghana, Guinea, Mali, Egypt, Morocco, Algeria) under Nkrumah wanted immediate political union with a continental government, common army and currency. The Monrovia group (Nigeria, Liberia, Ethiopia and most francophone states) preferred gradual functional cooperation while preserving sovereign equality and non-interference. The OAU Charter of 1963 largely reflected the Monrovia position; the AU's stronger institutions represent a partial, delayed victory for the Casablanca vision.

quiz.solution: Nkrumah's Casablanca group wanted a continental government at once.

options: Sirte, 1999
Lome, 2000

quiz.solution: The Union was inaugurated at the Durban summit in July 2002.

options: Intervene in grave circumstances
Print currency

quiz.solution: It allows intervention in cases of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.

options: Peace and Security Council

options: Addis Ababa
Midrand, South Africa
Abuja
Nairobi
quiz.solution: It sits at Midrand near Johannesburg.

options: Anglophone-francophone division
Excess intra-regional trade
Uniform currency
Absence of members
quiz.solution: Colonial heritage and rival groupings such as UEMOA weaken cohesion.

quiz.q: The proposed single ECOWAS currency is the:
options: Eco
Naira
CFA
Cedi
quiz.solution: The eco has been repeatedly postponed due to unmet convergence criteria.

quiz.q: The African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights was adopted in:
quiz.solution: It was adopted in Nairobi in 1981 and came into force in 1986.

quiz.q: ECOWAS restored the elected President of The Gambia in:
quiz.solution: ECOMIG deployment in January 2017 enforced Adama Barrow's election victory.

quiz.solution: The African Continental Free Trade Area began trading in January 2021.
